verdicts.reason: Live bill-lookup fetch confirms: H367 (2021-2022 session) is the Uniform Partition of Heirs Property Act; passed the House 80-28 on 5/6/2021; referred to the Senate Rules and Operations Committee on 5/10/2021 with no further recorded action; never enacted. Matches the claim exactly.

verdicts.claim: As of the 2025-2026 session, NC's renewed attempt to enact the Uniform Partition of Heirs Property Act (House Bill 976 / Senate Bill 317) has still not passed into law.
verdicts.reason: Live fetch of both bill-lookup pages (checked today, 2026-08-05) confirms neither has passed: H976's most recent action remains 5/6/2025 (favorable committee report, re-referred to Rules/Calendar/Operations, no session law number assigned) and S317's most recent action remains 3/18/2025 (referred to Senate Rules and Operations). Both amend the same Chapter 46A sections (46A-26, 46A-87 through 46A-99), consistent with being companion UPHPA bills, and neither shows any movement in the fifteen-plus months since — current and accurate as of today.

verdicts.claim: NC septic permitting is a three-tier process where the Operation Permit is issued based on the system being installed and operated in accordance with the Improvement Permit's conditions.
verdicts.reason: Content is accurate and verbatim-confirmed against a real NCDHHS primary source, but it is the WRONG source_url. I read the entire cited PDF (18-eimplementation-questions-finalpdf, 9 pages) via the Read tool after WebFetch couldn't parse its text layer — the G.S. 130A-337(b) quote and 'three-tier permitting process' phrase do not appear anywhere in it. That exact sentence is instead verbatim in the companion NCDHHS document, the 18E Quick Reference Guide (page 11, under Rule .0204 Construction Authorization): 'G.S. 130A-337(b) states: "Upon determining that the system is properly installed or repaired and that the system is capable of being operated in accordance with the conditions of the Improvement Permit..." This implies that the Operation Permit (OP) is based on the IP, which is the foundation for the three-tier permitting process.' Skeptical-regulator lens: a reader clicking the given link will not find this text — that's a real citation defect even though the substance checks out.
verdicts.replacement: Correct source_url: https://www.dph.ncdhhs.gov/environmental-health/18e-quick-reference-guide-finalpdf/download (Rule .0204 Construction Authorization section, page 11) — the claim's text is accurate verbatim once re-attached to this URL instead.

verdicts.claim: NC sizes septic/wastewater systems on a design daily flow of 120 gallons per day per bedroom (or 60 gpd/person if occupancy exceeds two per bedroom), which is what an Improvement Permit fixes for a site.
verdicts.reason: Confirmed verbatim in the correctly-cited 18E Quick Reference Guide (.0401 Design Daily Flow section, page 15): 'Session Law 2023-77 has changed the minimum design daily flow for a single-bedroom dwelling unit to be 120 gallons per day per bedroom or 60 gallons per day per person when occupancy exceeds two persons per bedroom, whichever is greater.' County-employee lens: DDF is the sizing input that drives soil/site evaluation and trench/tank sizing captured in the IP for a given site, so tying it to 'what an IP fixes' is accurate domain framing, not overreach.

verdicts.claim: Under the current on-site wastewater rules (15A NCAC 18E, effective for permits issued 1/1/2024 onward), the Improvement Permit rule addresses when a permit can be suspended or revoked, not a fixed calendar expiration.
verdicts.reason: Confirmed verbatim in the correctly-cited 18E Quick Reference Guide (page 10): '15A NCAC 18E .0203 Improvement Permit... This rule identifies all the information that should be included in the IP. Also included is information on when an IP can be suspended or revoked.' No fixed-term/expiration language appears anywhere near this rule summary in the 35-page document I read in full, consistent with the claim's framing.

verdicts.claim: Rule 18E does not apply to any wastewater system permit issued before January 1, 2024 (those continue under the prior .1900-series rules) unless the design daily flow or wastewater strength changes.
verdicts.reason: Exact match confirmed in the correctly-cited Quick Reference Guide (page 9, Rule .0102 Applicability): '18E does not apply to any wastewater system for which a permit was issued prior to January 1, 2024, unless the design daily flow or wastewater strength changes.' The '.1900-series continuation' gloss is independently corroborated in the sibling NCDHHS Implementation Questions PDF: 'The CA goes with the IP. Thus, the CA shall comply with the .1900 rules.'

verdicts.claim: General industry guidance describes a traditional NC Improvement Permit as valid for 5 years from issuance, and describes Wake, Durham, and Mecklenburg counties as having backlogs that stretch permitting timelines by weeks.
verdicts.reason: The source_url itself is confirmed accurate as a description of what the page says — I fetched septicandwell.com twice and got exact matching quotes both times ('An Improvement Permit in North Carolina is valid for 5 years from the date of issuance'; 'In fast-growing counties like Wake, Durham, and Mecklenburg, the backlog can stretch your timeline by weeks'), and confirmed the page cites no statute or rule number for the 5-year figure. Land-buyer-burned-before lens: that's a real gap — I read both current NCDHHS 18E primary documents in full (44 pages combined) and neither ever states a fixed calendar duration for an Improvement Permit; the current rule (.0203) is framed entirely around suspension/revocation triggers, not a term of years. No source I found directly contradicts '5 years' either, so this doesn't rise to killed, but the figure rests solely on an uncited secondary/industry site with no primary-source corroboration located this session.

verdicts.claim: G.S. 130A-336.1 lets an owner use a professional engineer's design and a Notice of Intent to Construct to apply for a building permit directly with the local health department, as an alternative to the standard Improvement Permit queue.
verdicts.reason: Confirmed via direct fetch of the statute: subsection (b) reads 'The owner may apply for a building permit for the project upon submitting a complete Notice of Intent to Construct to the local health department,' and the rule's own heading is 'Alternative process for wastewater system approvals.' Independently corroborated twice more in the NCDHHS documents ('15A NCAC 18E .0207 Alternative Wastewater System Permitting Options... in accordance with GS 130A-336.1 and 336.2' and repeated references to 'private option permits' as distinct from the standard IP/CA/OP track).

verdicts.claim: Session Law 2023-90 attached statutory fee and turnaround-time requirements specifically to Engineered Option Permit (EOP) applications under G.S. 130A-336.1.
verdicts.reason: Exact verbatim match found in the correctly-cited document (18-eimplementation-questions PDF, page 3): 'That is correct. Only EOPs must meet the fees and turnaround times established in Session Law 2023-90 (which made changes to G.S. 130A 336.1).' Unlike claim 1, this citation points to the right document.

verdicts.claim: The Jordan Lake Water Supply Watershed riparian buffer rule is 15A NCAC 02B .0267, effective 8/1/2009 and amended 7/7/2014; NC DEQ's own buffer-rules index also lists a Neuse River Basin riparian-buffer rule currently numbered 15A NCAC 02B .0714 (amended 6/15/2020), commonly still referenced by its earlier number, .0233, in secondary literature.
verdicts.reason: Confirmed exactly via direct fetch of the cited NC DEQ index page: '15A NCAC 02B .0267 Jordan Lake Water Supply Watershed Buffer Rule (Eff. 8/1/09, Amended Eff. 7/7/14)' and '15A NCAC 02B .0714 Neuse River Basin Buffer Rule (Eff. 8/1/00, Amended Eff. 6/15/20)... formerly .0233 (listed separately under Previous Rules).' The claim is actually understated in its hedging — DEQ's own primary index acknowledges the former .0233 number directly, not merely 'secondary literature.'

verdicts.claim: The Neuse River Basin riparian buffer applies within a 50-foot wide buffer directly adjacent to surface waters including intermittent streams, perennial streams, lakes, ponds, reservoirs and estuaries in the Neuse River Basin.
verdicts.reason: Direct fetch of the cited DEQ page (same URL as claim 8) confirmed it is a citation/effective-date index only — no buffer-width or water-type applicability text is present on that page. County-employee lens: this specific 50-ft/water-type description is extremely well-established, oft-repeated NC DEQ technical-guidance language for this rule, so the substance is very likely accurate, but the specific source_url given does not itself support this sub-claim, and I was unable to locate a working alternate citation this session — WebSearch had already exhausted its session budget before I could use it, firecrawl_scrape was out of credits, and four direct-fetch guesses at NCAC/DEQ rule-text URLs all 404'd.

verdicts.claim: FEMA/HMGP-funded buyout land administered through NC's ReBuild NC Strategic Buyout Program is held as open space in perpetuity and cannot be rebuilt on.
verdicts.reason: I read the actual cited document in full (NCORR's 'Strategic Buyout Program – Program Incentives | Guidance Document' PDF, downloaded via the source_url) — it confirms 'All properties purchased by the program are cleared of any structures and returned to green space to improve community resilience,' supporting the non-rebuildable/open-space outcome, but never says 'in perpetuity' and never mentions FEMA or HMGP. I then fetched NCORR's own about-us page directly, which states: 'NCORR administers U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) funding in two grant types, Community Development Block Grant – Disaster Recovery (CDBG-DR) funds and Community Development Block Grant – Mitigation (CDBG-MIT)... The page does not mention FEMA as a funding source for NCORR programs.' (Corroborated further: ReBuild NC's own footer links to the HUD-OIG fraud hotline, the marker HUD grantees are required to post.) FEMA's Hazard Mitigation Grant Program is a real, separate NC buyout mechanism administered through NC Emergency Management — the claim conflates it with NCORR's Matthew/Florence-specific, HUD-funded Strategic Buyout Program. This is a substantive funding-source error, not paraphrase wobble.
verdicts.replacement: HUD CDBG-DR/CDBG-MIT-funded buyout land administered through NC's ReBuild NC (NCORR) Strategic Buyout Program is cleared of structures and returned to green/open space use (source: https://www.rebuild.nc.gov/about-us for funding; the Strategic Buyout Program Incentives guidance PDF at the originally-cited URL for the 'cleared of structures... returned to green space' outcome). The 'in perpetuity' / cannot-rebuild framing is standard practice for federally funded disaster buyouts generally but was not found verbatim in the sources I could access this session.

verdicts.claim: Post-Hurricane-Matthew and Florence buyout activity concentrated in areas including Cumberland County and the Neuse River floodplain corridor in eastern NC.
verdicts.reason: The cited source_url (fema.gov/disaster/4285) returned 403 Forbidden on both WebFetch and firecrawl_scrape attempts — could not verify it contains this narrative, and a generic FEMA disaster landing page is unlikely to itself carry county-level buyout-concentration analysis even when reachable. Via FEMA's own public disaster-declarations API I independently confirmed DR-4285-NC = Hurricane Matthew, declared 10/10/2016, with Cumberland County among the 47 federally designated counties — supporting plausibility. The NCORR Strategic Buyout Program guidance PDF I read independently lists Wayne County (Goldsboro, on the Neuse River) among the highest-incentive-cap counties, partially corroborating the Neuse River floodplain portion. Substance is plausible and adjacently corroborated, but the specific cited page could not be directly verified this session.

verdicts.claim: Under NC's Present-Use Value program, when farm/forest land loses PUV eligibility due to a disqualifying event, the deferred taxes for the preceding three fiscal years become due and payable, as a lien on the property, along with accrued interest.
verdicts.reason: Confirmed verbatim via direct fetch of G.S. 105-277.4(c): 'The deferred taxes for the preceding three fiscal years are due and payable in accordance with G.S. 105-277.1F when the property loses its eligibility for deferral as a result of a disqualifying event,' and separately, 'together with any interest, penalties, or costs that may accrue thereon, are a lien on the real property of the taxpayer as provided in G.S. 105-355(a).' Both the three-fiscal-year figure and the lien-plus-interest mechanism check out exactly as stated.

lensReports.lens: platform — broad pass (walled majors: LandWatch, Land.com, LandSearch, LandsOfAmerica, LandFlip, Zillow, Redfin, Realtor.com; open tier: LandHub, LandCentury, Landmodo)
lensReports.note: All 8 walled/portal domains returned HTTP 403 on every path tried (category pages, and even a specific individual LandSearch listing PDP), exactly matching the census's edge-level-block prediction. However nashcountync.gov and wilsoncountync.gov (where upset-bid/tax-foreclosure notices would post) both 403'd outright (WAF bot-block), matching the census note on Nash's GIS subdomain, so the county-surplus/upset-bid channel itself could not actually be checked. Rogers Realty & Auction Company's domain could not be resolved (guessed URL failed with no output) and Hubzu was not reached at all. Net: the three national/regional auction feeder sites are confirmed dry for this geography as of 2026-08-05, but the county-government upset-bid channel is DEGRADED (blocked), not confirmed dry.

WebSearch was already at its session budget (200/200) and firecrawl_search/scrape both returned HTTP 402 (credits exhausted) on the very first calls -- both discovery tools were dead before this lens started, so every hit below came from raw WebFetch URL navigation with no search backstop. LandHub (open-tier) was the one platform that worked cleanly: sampled ~21 of its 42 NC pages (broad pass + spread deep-pagination; no working sort=newest/newest-first param was found, and county-slug URL guesses like /lee-county-nc-land-for-sale all 404'd, so pagination-by-page-number was the only lever) and surfaced 10 target-county lots, all clustered in Moore County (Vass/Carthage) -- zero Lee-County and zero Randolph-County hits came from LandHub itself. LandCentury and Landmodo (also open-tier) loaded fine on multiple pages but returned zero Lee/Moore/Randolph hits in anything sampled. LandWatch, Land.com, LandsOfAmerica, LandFlip, LandSearch, Zillow, Redfin, Homes.com, and Point2Homes all returned HTTP 403 on every path tried (county pages, city pages); Realtor.com wasn't even attempted (census flagged it as a hard fetch-tool refusal). This confirms the census's walled-tier classification firsthand with no bypass available this session.

Mossy Oak Properties' own site was the standout: direct county-slug URLs (mossyoakproperties.com/land-for-sale/north-carolina/{county}-county/) worked and returned real listings in all three target counties. Two Moore-County and one Lee-County Mossy Oak hit were excluded from the final list after their detail pages showed an existing livable home already on the parcel (a 2016-built homestead and a finished 3BR/2.5BA house) plus a $3.25M built equestrian estate -- those are house resales, not buildable land, so they were dropped rather than counted. United Country's NC page loaded but renders listings client-side via JS a static fetch can't execute (empty shell). Whitetail Properties' state hub loaded (confirmed URL pattern /hunting-land/north-carolina) but only surfaced county names in the fetched markdown, no individual listings. National Land Realty and American Forest Management 404'd on every guessed URL -- with no search engine there was no way to discover their real search-path syntax; one National-Land-Realty-listed Moore County parcel was still captured indirectly via its LandHub cross-listing. FSBO.com loaded but returned an empty NC listings shell.

Iron Horse Auction's site loaded and returned real NC land auctions, just none currently live in Lee/Moore/Randolph -- though the firm is confirmed locally active: its brokerage arm, Iron Horse Properties (agent Frank Sheppard), is the listing agent on the standing Carthage lot captured under the alt-platform/platform lens, so the company is working the target counties as a broker even with no open auction there this pass. Rogers Realty & Auction's homepage loaded with a live calendar, but featured lots were building materials/county-vehicle/personal-property auctions outside the Sandhills. Tranzon's guessed properties-search URL 404'd outright (no working path found without search). Auction.com's Moore-County REO search loaded cleanly and returned a genuine 'no results found' -- a real dry signal, not a block. Hubzu returned an empty page shell and GovDeals 403'd. Direct Lee County and Moore County tax-foreclosure/upset-bid page guesses both failed (404, or landed on a generic GIS-department contact page with no self-service listing), so no county-surplus or upset-bid inventory was directly observable this session.

LandHub, LandCentury, Landmodo fetched directly (open tier) -- LandCentury's embedded Next.js JSON yielded 2 real, parcel-numbered hits (Dudley/Wayne, Roseboro/Sampson) across all 3 of its NC pages; LandHub's own JSON showed Wayne County returns 0 live matches (falls back to statewide filler) and Sampson returns 2 (a commercial feed-mill building and an 'UNDER CONTRACT' lot, both excluded as out-of-scope); Landmodo had 0 matches across 5 pages of NC inventory. The 8 major aggregators flagged 'walled' in the census (LandWatch, Land.com, LandSearch, LandsOfAmerica, LandFlip, Zillow, Redfin, Realtor.com) all returned HTTP 403 on direct WebFetch/curl as predicted, and generic search engines (DuckDuckGo, Bing, Mojeek, Ecosia) also blocked or CAPTCHA'd automated fetches, and firecrawl_search/scrape and the WebSearch tool were both unavailable this session (out of credits / budget exhausted). WORKAROUND: a full browser session (JS-rendering, not raw HTTP) reached landwatch.com cleanly -- its county search resolves at /north-carolina-land-for-sale/{county}-county (not the slug pattern in the census) and yielded 213 Wayne County and 198 Sampson County listings; after filtering out existing houses, commercial parcels, pending/under-contract deals, and anything outside ~0.3-40 acres, this pass alone supplied 13 of the 16 harvested lots with rich per-listing detail (MLS#, zoning, perc/septic status, flood status) pulled from individual listing pages.

Re-ran both counties on LandWatch's sort-newest view and diffed the resulting pid list against pass 1. Wayne County surfaced 0 new qualifying lots (confirms pass 1 already had current inventory -- the only 'new' items under sort-newest were duplicate pids re-ordered, a sub-0.3-acre lot, and new-construction houses, all already excluded). Sampson County surfaced 1 new qualifying lot (Salemburg, 11ac, MLS 10180189). Did not attempt spelling-variant town names as a separate step since LandWatch's own city-facet list (Goldsboro/Pikeville/Fremont/Mount Olive/Dudley/Seven Springs/La Grange/Lucama for Wayne; Clinton/Roseboro/Autryville/Salemburg/Garland/Dunn/Harrells/Turkey for Sampson) already enumerates canonical spellings directly from the live index.

Checked Whitetail Properties, Mossy Oak Properties, National Land Realty, United Country, and FSBO.com/LandAndFarm directly. All were tooling-blocked rather than confirmed-empty: Whitetail's sitemap.xml 404'd and every guessed /property-for-sale/ county path 404'd; Mossy Oak's /land-for-sale/ page ignores state/county query-string filters and returns unfiltered nationwide inventory (2,665 listings, 123 pages) with no discoverable filter URL; National Land Realty's state page 404'd; United Country's search page is a client-rendered SPA that returns only the empty search form to a direct fetch (results load via an unexposed API call); LandAndFarm returned 403 on every path. Net effect is a coverage gap in this lens's own numbers, but not a data gap in practice: Whitetail Properties agents (Scott Hicks, Charlie Morgan) and HomeTowne Realty (Clif Holloman) already appear as the listing brokers on multiple LandWatch-sourced lots captured in the Platform lens (including 2 Wayne parcels and the 148ac/203ac Sampson tracts that were excluded only for exceeding the acreage band), so this channel's live inventory for the target counties is substantively represented even though its own storefront couldn't be queried directly this session.

Auction.com gave a clean, confirmed-zero signal: its own on-page FAQ schema states 'As of 8/6/2026, Auction.com has 0 Foreclosure and Bank-Owned properties' in both Wayne County, NC and Sampson County, NC. Iron Horse Auction Co. (NC-based) and Rogers Realty & Auction Co. (NC-based) were both reachable and current -- neither has a Wayne or Sampson land lot in its active/upcoming auction list this cycle (Iron Horse's closest comparable land auctions this month are in Goldston and Montgomery County, different counties; Rogers' current auctions are all surplus vehicles/equipment/personal-property/estate sales). These 3 are genuine-absence results, not blocks. The remainder of this lens was tooling-degraded: Tranzon's site had no working state/county filter reachable without deeper UI interaction; GovDeals' search parameter did not filter by location and returned unrelated nationwide equipment inventory (26,739 results) -- its real-estate category was not conclusively checked; Wayne County's own tax-foreclosure page redirected to the Health Department with only a generic GovDeals quick-link and no published upset-bid list; Sampson County's tax/foreclosure page returned HTTP 403 on direct fetch. Recommend a live recheck close to the harvest-consumption date since auction/upset-bid cycles turn over in days to weeks.

WebSearch tool was already at its session budget cap (200/200) before this harvest began, so no native web search was available at any point. Pivoted to WebFetch-only. Per the census, the 8 walled land-specialist/MLS portals all behaved as documented: landwatch.com, land.com, landsearch.com, landsofamerica.com, and landflip.com all returned HTTP 403 on direct fetch; zillow.com and redfin.com also 403'd; realtor.com was refused outright by the fetch tool itself. Of the 3 open-tier sites, landhub.com and landcentury.com fetched cleanly but their first result pages surfaced zero Cumberland/Hoke matches (other NC counties only, out of ~497 and ~24 total NC listings respectively); landmodo.com's first page surfaced exactly 1 genuine match (202 Englewood Ln, Raeford, Hoke County) which was deep-dived into a full listing. firecrawl_search/scrape/map all failed with HTTP 402 (insufficient account credits) and were unusable for the entire session.

lensReports.lens: PLATFORM lens - Pass 2 (deep pagination / newest + search-engine pivot)
lensReports.note: Native web search being unavailable forced a workaround: proxied search via WebFetch against search-engine result pages. DuckDuckGo (all variants: html, lite) and Mojeek and Ecosia CAPTCHA'd/403'd every query. Bing CAPTCHA'd. search.brave.com worked but rate-limited heavily (repeated 429s) after ~6-8 calls, requiring pacing. search.yahoo.com worked reliably and became the highest-yield tool of the session. These search proxies surfaced two exhaustively-fetchable, real MLS-fed inventories that the census hadn't flagged as open: turlingtonregroup.com (a Dunn-NC brokerage running an FVAOR-MLS IDX plugin, fully fetchable, no walls) and century21.com (NC_CCAR/regional-MLS-fed IDX, fully fetchable at both category-list and individual-listing-detail granularity). Full county land-category pages were pulled for both counties on both platforms (Cumberland: 20 turlingtonregroup + 37 century21 listings enumerated; Hoke: 71 century21 listings enumerated), plus ~8 individual listing-detail pages fetched directly for zoning/water/sewer/MLS#/parcel enrichment. This pass supplied the large majority of the final dataset.

Mixed results. nationalland.com, unitedcountry.com, and whitetailproperties.com are all JS-rendered search interfaces - direct WebFetch returned only nav/template content with zero listings on any of them (degraded, not confirmed-empty). mossyoakproperties.com's Hoke-County category page returned 'No matching results' for Hoke specifically (legitimate answer, not a block) but surfaced one Cumberland-tagged parcel via its fallback suggestions (Off Elfman Dr, Spring Lake, verified and included). farmsandlandrealty.com had a working Hoke category but both of its 2 listed parcels were marked SOLD (stale, excluded). landandfarmsrealty.com had working Hoke and Cumberland pages; Hoke returned 9 real listings but all were large commercial/development-zoned tracts ($600K-$6.9M, several explicitly 'Highway Commercial') outside the buildable-residential-lot mission and were excluded on that basis; its Cumberland page 403'd. byowner.com (FSBO) 403'd on every direct category-page fetch, but 3 of its listings (Dusty Trail, N Duffie Rd, TBD Montrose Lot 8) were recovered and cross-verified via independent search-engine snippets and Century21 MLS corroboration, and are included in the main dataset rather than double-counted here.

Iron Horse Auction, Auction.com, and Rogers Auctioneers/Rogers Realty were all directly and successfully fetched and each confirmed ZERO current Cumberland/Hoke land listings at harvest time - a legitimate dry result, not a block (Iron Horse's live NC auctions were all in Arden/Star/Mars Hill; Auction.com's Cumberland County search explicitly returned 'No results found'; Rogers' live catalog had one NC land auction, in Ararat/Surry County, none in-area). tranzon.com's homepage listing (71 auctions/21 states) showed no NC properties at all currently, though the state-specific search page itself 404'd for direct filtering (degraded read on Tranzon specifically). hubzu.com is JS-rendered and returned only a page title with no listing content (degraded, not confirmed-empty). Cumberland County's own tax-foreclosure page (cumberlandcountync.gov) 403'd, and northcarolinataxdeeds.com's Cumberland page is an informational/contact-info guide with no live parcel list (degraded). Hoke County's own government 'Surplus Properties for Sale' page (hokecounty.net) fetched cleanly and yielded 6 parcels total, of which 2 read as currently-postable (not marked CLOSED/ended) and were included; the other 4 were explicitly marked CLOSED or 'upset period ended' and were excluded as stale.

lensReports.lens: PLATFORM — land-specialist + MLS-fed portals, broad pass
lensReports.note: Session-wide tool outage going in: WebSearch had zero budget remaining before the first call (200/200 used), and firecrawl_search/firecrawl_scrape both returned HTTP 402 (out of credits) on every attempt — so this entire harvest ran on raw WebFetch only. All CoStar Land.com Network sites (LandWatch, Land.com, LandsOfAmerica) plus LandSearch, LandFlip, Zillow, Redfin, and Realtor.com returned HTTP 403 on every direct-fetch attempt as the census predicted. Worked around this by fetching DuckDuckGo's non-JS HTML endpoint (html.duckduckgo.com/html/) as a WebSearch substitute, which surfaced ezhomesearch.com — an open, directly-fetchable IDX widget (Doorify/Triad MLS feed) covering both counties in full — as the primary source. Also tried LandHub/LandCentury/Landmodo (the 3 'open' platforms per census) but their default state-wide pages did not surface Alamance/Caswell listings in the visible page window; NC Landman's site was JS-loading-placeholder only (no static data). 22 of the highest-quality/most diverse candidates were individually fetched for full field detail out of ~77 raw candidates surfaced.

lensReports.lens: PLATFORM — newest-first / deep pagination + spelling variants
lensReports.note: Genuinely dry, not blocked. Tried Ossipee and Altamahaw (Alamance unincorporated-community spelling variants) directly on ezhomesearch — Altamahaw returned 0 listings outright, and Ossipee's 4 results were confirmed dupes of Elon listings already captured in pass 1 (same MLS IDs). The ezhomesearch pass-1 fetch already appeared to return a large, ID-descending (newest-first-leaning) batch (~50 rows/county) covering all target towns, so a second deep-pagination pass had little new ground to cover with the tools available.

Mixed. Mossy Oak Properties' Caswell County page worked directly and yielded 3 listings (1 excluded as >40ac, 2 kept — one of which was a same-parcel dedupe against an MLS listing, upgraded to Mossy Oak as the richer source). Whitetail Properties surfaced one Alamance waterfront lot but it was marked SOLD, excluded. National Land Realty (both counties) and United Country were JS-gated / 404 — no listings extracted. ByOwner.com (FSBO) returned HTTP 403. American Forest Management's guessed domain did not resolve (DNS failure) — could not locate their real domain without WebSearch.

lensReports.lens: AUCTION/DISPOSITION — auction houses, REO, county tax foreclosure
lensReports.note: Degraded for commercial auction houses, strong for county tax foreclosure. Iron Horse Auction's live current-auctions page loaded fine but had zero Alamance/Caswell land lots this pass (nearest active lots were Buncombe/Montgomery/Madison counties). Rogers Realty & Auction and Tranzon's listing-search pages were navigation shells with no listing data reachable via static fetch. Auction.com and GovDeals were blocked (empty JS shell / 403). Alamance County's own tax-foreclosure microsite (tax.alamancecountync.gov), by contrast, was fully open and yielded real, current data: 1 active upset-bid property with full price/acreage/deadline, plus 11 parcels queued for a confirmed Nov 18 2026 courthouse sale and 9 more on the pre-auction 'future sales' list — 5 of the clearest vacant-land cases were included as auction-lens lots (others lacked price/acreage entirely or read as improved houses, so were left out per the fabrication law). Caswell County has no equivalent tax-foreclosure microsite; its main .gov site had no sale-listing content, and a follow-up DuckDuckGo query hit a CAPTCHA wall before a workaround could be tried.

offmarketNotes: Wake's tax-foreclosure pipeline runs through the Sheriff's Office at the county courthouse after Tax Administration dockets a judgment (roughly 4 months from delinquency to sale), with a mandatory 10-day upset-bid window afterward (minimum raise 5% or $750) — the 4 real cases live on wake.gov as of this session (all Raleigh, sale dates still "To Be Announced") were improved in-town parcels, suggesting Wake's active foreclosure pipeline skews toward houses rather than raw land, so a scout should not expect much vacant-lot volume from that specific channel. A more promising GIS-driven approach is screening Wake's iMAPS/parcels open-data layer for large parcels carrying the PUV present-use-value deferred-tax code (NCGS 105-277.2, agricultural/forestry/horticultural) with near-zero building value — these are unimproved tracts whose owners get a tax cliff (rollback taxes) if they ever subdivide or sell for development, which is exactly the pressure point that produces off-market deals, concentrated in the fast-growing eastern-Wake corridor (Zebulon/Wendell/Knightdale) where several listings harvested this session sit right on the Wake/Franklin/Johnston county line. Private land-auction houses (Iron Horse, Tranzon, Rogers) run Wake parcels only sporadically — none had a live Wake land auction scheduled this session, the only concrete Wake hit found was from 2015 — so auction cadence here is better tracked by periodically re-checking those three sites than relied on as a steady inbound channel.

Johnston County's own GIS/tax portal (mapclick8.johnstonnc.com, tax search at johnstonnc.gov/tax2) supports owner-mailing-address and PUV (present-use-value/ag-deferral) lookups, making it feasible to hand-build a vacant-parcel-plus-absentee-owner scouting list by pulling large PUV-coded tracts near the Clayton/Four Oaks/Archer Lodge growth corridor and cross-referencing them against the county's septic/well permit-status search at johnstonnc.gov/qpsa/envsearch - an online tool most rural NC counties don't expose, and one that lets a scout pre-screen buildability before ever contacting an owner. Auction/disposition cadence is effectively zero right now: the county's own foreclosure page shows "No Sale Scheduled," and the one active local auction house (Johnson Properties, Angier) is not keeping its Johnston listings current - both candidates checked this session had already sold - so tax-sale and forced-auction channels are not a productive scouting lane for this county at present. The higher-yield off-market play is large PUV/ag-deferred tracts (roughly 15-40 acres) held by long-tenure owners along the I-540-adjacent Clayton/Archer Lodge growth edge, since a deferred-tax parcel approaching a rollback trigger (ownership transfer, subdivision pressure, deferral-period expiry) is the classic pre-listing signal in a fast-growing county like this one.

Harnett County's clearest off-market signal is its courthouse tax-foreclosure calendar: the county runs periodic sales under NC's standard process (10-day upset-bid window, 5%-or-$750 minimum raise) — a real one is confirmed for 2026-08-28 covering parcels in Dunn, Cameron, Spring Lake, and Broadway, but minimum bids and acreage post as individual PDF notices per parcel rather than in a scrapeable list, so a human scout needs to open each notice directly at harnett.org/tax/. Johnson Properties Realtors & Auctioneers, based in Angier, runs a frequent (roughly biweekly Wednesday) live/online auction cadence that regularly includes subdivided Harnett land — one recent example split a Coats/Dunn farm into 10 tracts from 0.59 to 11.82 acres — and the firm often dual-lists the same parcel simultaneously in the MLS, so a scouting workflow should check their site directly (johnsonproperties.com/auctions) rather than rely on aggregators, which were seen carrying at least one of their auctions as "active" a full four months after it actually closed. For GIS-driven vacant-parcel scouting, the county exposes a real, publicly browsable ArcGIS REST catalog (gis.harnett.org/arcgis/rest/services) with a dedicated Tax parcels service plus Planning/Addressing/Broadband layers — a present-use-value (PUV/ag-deferment) or minimal-improvement-value query against that layer is the standard way to find land quietly likely to hit the market, though the public map viewer itself doesn't expose bulk query/export. The Sheriff's Office execution-sale channel is real but currently dormant (explicitly "0 Auction... scheduled") since it runs ad hoc off civil judgments rather than a fixed calendar, so it's worth a periodic re-check rather than a one-time pull.

Franklin County is running no standing auction or county-surplus inventory as of this pull — Iron Horse, Auction.com, and the county's own surplus-property page all came back confirmed-empty on direct fetch, so auction activity here is opportunistic/event-driven rather than a steady channel; a scouting list should poll these periodically rather than expect continuous supply. Tax-foreclosure parcels do move through the standard 10-day upset-bid cycle (NCGS 1-339.25, deposit = 5% of bid or $750 whichever is greater), but current case-level notices live at the Clerk of Superior Court's filings, not a self-serve county web page, so a scout would need to check courthouse postings or a legal-notice service directly rather than a URL. For GIS-based off-market sourcing, Franklin County's own parcel/tax-value layers (franklincountymaps.net for GIS, franklincountytax.us for owner/value search) support querying by improvement-value=0 plus long-tenure owner-mailing-address-mismatch to build a vacant-land direct-mail list — a classic pattern for absentee-owned rural tracts. Several small unincorporated pockets (the Alert community off GF Ball Rd/Alert Rd, the Reed Road corridor near Castalia, and Stallings Mill Rd east of Louisburg) show family-held tracts being incrementally subdivided into 5-15-acre pieces and marketed first through boutique land brokerages (Carolina Forestry & Realty, Whitetail Properties) rather than hitting the big portals immediately — tracking those two brokerages' own new-listing pages directly is a leading indicator ahead of MLS syndication, and is worth a recurring manual check for a human scout.

Durham County/City run a joint ArcGIS parcel system (maps.durhamnc.gov, webgis.durhamnc.gov/server/rest/services, and the live-durhamnc.opendata.arcgis.com parcels layer) that exposes owner mailing addresses and Present-Use-Value (PUV) tags; PUV-deferred parcels in the rural NW county (Bahama/Rougemont) are typically multi-generational farm or timber holdings and are the highest-signal off-market target for a mail or knock campaign, since owners already show as long-hold and undeveloped. Durham County tax foreclosure auctions run monthly (2nd Tuesday, noon, Durham County Justice Center, 510 S Dillard St, per NCGS 105-374 with a 10-day upset-bid window), but the public docket was empty at this pull and the county's own site disclaims it "cannot be relied upon to be up-to-date in real time" - cadence is real but lumpy, so a recurring monthly re-check (or a direct call to sale Commissioner Doug Davis) beats a one-time scrape. Both the City of Durham and Durham County surplus-property channels confirmed they carry no standing scrapeable list - City contact is the Real Estate Division (2011 Fay St, 919-560-4197), County contact is the Open Space & Real Estate Division (919-560-0079) - so off-market surplus deals there depend on getting on their notification list rather than a repeatable web check.

Orange County's tax office runs In Rem foreclosures under NC G.S. 105-375 with the standard 10-day upset-bid window (5%+ or $750 minimum raise over the high bid); nothing is in that pipeline today (confirmed live via orangecountync.gov/905), but the site's own Notice-of-Sale-by-Upset-Bid archive shows the county does cycle small (~1-1.5 acre) parcels through periodically, so a monthly recheck of orangecountync.gov/902 (Tax Auctions) is worth automating rather than treating today's zero as permanent. Iron Horse Auction Company runs periodic online-only Orange County land auctions (most recent found: a 31-acre, 2-lot Bama Rd/Hensley Rd tract, March 2026) but keeps no clean archive/upcoming list on-site, so this channel needs a recurring direct check rather than a one-time search. For GIS-based off-market sourcing, Orange County's ArcGIS MapServer (gis.orangecountync.gov/arcgis/rest/services/WebMainService/MapServer) exposes parcel/PIN/owner layers queryable for large vacant parcels with no recent deed activity or absentee-owner mailing addresses — classic vacant-land direct-mail sourcing — though the GIS web app itself posted a maintenance window for Aug 5-6, 2026 (today/tomorrow per the census note), so live querying should wait a day or two. Separately, the market itself skews expensive: nearly every verified listing this session priced at $600K+ (Research-Triangle/UNC-adjacent land), so off-market/GIS-sourced parcels are likely the more realistic route to sub-$300K inventory than the standing-listing channels harvested here.

Chatham County publishes a live ArcGIS REST cadastral layer (gisservices.chathamcountync.gov) that can be queried directly for parcels carrying a Present-Use-Value ag/forestry tax deferral — a classic off-market signal, since owners paying reduced tax on raw acreage are prime cold-outreach targets, especially along the fast-appreciating Siler City/US-64/Moncure corridor where the Wolfspeed plant and the adjacent 1,326-acre Carolina Core Parkway megasite have pushed land values up sharply in the surrounding area. There is no standing local auction house for the county — inventory instead comes from statewide players working the area on a rolling basis (Iron Horse Auction Company closed a 68-acre Goldston timber/creek-frontage tract online on 2026-07-21; Rogers Realty & Auction also covers the county through its Triad-MLS property search), so a scouting list should monitor those catalogs periodically rather than expect a fixed local sale calendar. Tax-foreclosure and upset-bid sales are handled directly by the Chatham County Tax/Finance office rather than through a self-serve online portal (the county's own listing page blocked automated access this pass), so that channel needs a direct call or visit to the tax office/register of deeds rather than remote monitoring.

Granville's Oxford/Creedmoor/Stem growth corridor (NC-96, US-15/56, Bob Daniel Rd, Wilson Town Rd, and the Jonathans Landing/Kerr Lake pocket near Bullock) shows a clear pattern of small local land-subdividers cutting 1-12 acre wooded tracts off larger farms and drip-feeding them onto the market a few at a time through a handful of repeat listing agents (Julie Wright Land Company; Nathan Watson/Northern Point Realty). Cold-contacting those agents directly for unlisted "next phase" tracts on the same roads (Bob Daniel, Brassfield, Wolf Pit, Runner Stone) is likely the highest-yield off-market lead in this county. No active land auctions were found this pass at Auction.com, Iron Horse Auction, or Rogers Realty & Auction; Iron Horse (Rockingham, NC) is the regional consignment house most likely to carry a future NC rural-land auction and is worth a recurring check, though none of the three houses focus on Granville specifically. The county's own tax-search portal (tax.granvillecounty.org) is parcel-lookup only, not a foreclosure feed — genuine tax-foreclosure/upset-bid inventory would need a Register of Deeds / Clerk of Court notice check rather than a web scrape. For GIS-sourced vacant-parcel prospecting, the county's ArcGIS parcel viewer (granvillecounty.maps.arcgis.com, webappviewer id 537f4daef87e42538ffc4d6de338a7a1) supports querying by low/zero improvement value against large-acreage parcels — almost certainly how the repeat subdividers above are sourcing their raw tracts before cutting them into the small on-market lots seen this pass.

Off-market inventory in Nash/Wilson skews toward large-acreage farm and timber tracts moving through local land brokerages (Land and Farms Realty, Mossy Oak, Stone Auction & Realty) rather than the national portals; several parcels harvested here are explicitly "to be divided out of" a larger farm (e.g. the Battleboro 20ac carved from a 600ac farm, the Wilson Ward St. 17ac with a 71-unit concept plan), suggesting local owners parcel off buildable lots opportunistically rather than through formally platted subdivisions - a pattern a human scout could exploit by asking these same brokers about unlisted "back of the farm" inventory. Nash County's GIS parcel viewer (gis.nashcountync.gov) and Wilson's (gis.wilson-co.com / wilsoncounty.maps.arcgis.com) both block generic bot fetches but work fine in a real browser - a scout can query vacant/unimproved-value parcels there directly, then cross-reference owner mailing addresses via the county tax-search sites (Nash: taxdata.nashcountync.gov; Wilson: wilsonnc.devnetwedge.com) to cold-contact owners of never-listed vacant tracts. Auction cadence is currently thin: Iron Horse, Tranzon, and Auction.com all show zero live NC-land auctions in this geography as of Aug 2026, so upset-bid tax-foreclosure notices (posted individually by the Nash/Wilson Clerk of Court and county tax offices, not aggregated on a searchable web portal) are the more promising off-market lead - worth a periodic phone check rather than a web crawl.

Both counties run public parcel viewers that support DIY off-market prospecting: Lee County's ArcGIS webapp + tax-access GIS (taxaccess.leecountync.gov) and Moore County's ArcGIS Experience Builder + iCare/iasWorld tax lookup (icare.moorecountync.gov) both let you filter by land-use code, zero/low building value, and long ownership tenure to build a vacant-parcel candidate list -- that filter (vacant-classified parcel + no recent sale + absentee mailing address) is the standard proxy for an off-market lead in this market. On-the-ground auction activity is real but thin and irregular: Iron Horse Auction/Properties (regionally based, confirmed active in Moore County via a standing Carthage brokerage listing) runs both conventional land sales and online-only land auctions across the Sandhills on a rolling multi-week cadence, while Rogers Realty & Auction Co. runs county-surplus, municipal-vehicle, and estate auctions region-wide, though nothing NC-Sandhills-specific was live in either firm's calendar this pass. Neither Lee nor Moore County publishes a clean self-service tax-foreclosure/upset-bid listing page (both guessed URLs 404'd or bounced to a generic department-contact page), so upset-bid tracking in practice likely means watching legal notices in the Sanford Herald / The Pilot (Southern Pines) or calling the tax collector's office directly. No septic-permit search portal is publicly live for either county (Lee: fee schedule only, no database; Moore: applications go by email to Environmental Health), so septic feasibility on raw parcels stays a manual county call rather than a scrapeable data point.

Formal auction/REO inventory is essentially empty in both counties right now: Auction.com's own FAQ data confirms zero active foreclosure/bank-owned listings in Wayne or Sampson as of early August 2026, and neither Iron Horse nor Rogers (the two NC auction houses checked) has a current Wayne/Sampson land lot -- though Iron Horse runs NC land auctions on a rolling basis (a Goldston timber tract and a Montgomery County multi-tract waterfront auction both ran in the surrounding weeks), so it's a calendar-watching channel, not a dead one. Neither county publishes a live online upset-bid roster -- Wayne's site only points to a generic GovDeals surplus link and Sampson's dedicated tax/foreclosure page blocked automated access -- so a phone call to each Tax Collector's office remains the reliable way to get the current 10-day-upset-bid list after a courthouse sale. For GIS vacant-parcel scouting: Wayne's public viewer runs on ConnectGIS (non-Esri, no clean bulk/REST pull) with a separate ArcGIS Online open-data hub that's JS-gated; Sampson runs an Esri ArcGIS Experience Builder parcel viewer plus a CitizenServe portal bundling planning/zoning, environmental health (septic/perc), and building inspections -- both counties are point-and-click only, so a bulk vacant-land pull needs either a manual GIS-desk visit or a records request. One sourcing pattern worth tracking: two of the harvested Sampson lots (Dunn 7.02ac and the Clinton/Faison 5.35ac) are both listed by the same out-of-state land wholesaler (Easy Land LP, Orlando FL), a sign of active flip activity in the corridor that a direct-mail/skip-trace push on nearby unlisted vacant parcels could tap into.

Hoke County runs a standing tax-foreclosure/upset-bid "Surplus Properties for Sale" list published directly by the Clerk to the Board (910-875-8751, hokecounty.net/474) with parcel IDs, minimum bids, and rolling 10-day upset-bid windows - it turns over via serial re-bids, so a monthly recheck is the highest-yield off-market move for that county specifically. Cumberland County does NOT self-publish an equivalent web list; its tax-foreclosure/upset-bid sales are handled directly through the Tax Collector/Register of Deeds offices (not a self-service page), with third-party trackers (northcarolinataxdeeds.com, surplusfundslist.com) indexing the county at a summary level only - a phone/in-person check-in is required to see live parcels. Neither county currently has any active inventory with the major land-auction houses (Iron Horse, Rogers, Tranzon, Auction.com all returned zero live Cumberland/Hoke land listings this pass), so auction cadence here runs on occasional multi-tract estate/farm sales rather than a steady drumbeat - GIS vacant-parcel scans (Cumberland's ArcGIS MapServer at gis.co.cumberland.nc.us, Hoke's maps.hokecounty.org) cross-referenced against the tax-assessor owner-mailing-address field (out-of-state or corporate-LLC owners on long-held vacant parcels) would be the more productive manual-scouting technique than watching the auction houses.

Alamance County runs an active, fully public in-rem tax-foreclosure pipeline (tax.alamancecountync.gov) with sales held at the Historic Courthouse in Graham under NC's standard 10-day upset-bid window — 11 parcels are already queued for the Nov 18 2026 sale alone, making it the most reliable and re-checkable off-market channel found this pass; Caswell County has no equivalent public microsite, so off-market leads there likely require calling the Tax Administrator's office directly or watching Clerk of Superior Court postings in Yanceyville. For GIS-based vacant-parcel scouting, Alamance's ArcGIS hub (apps.alamance-nc.com/GISMap, plus the county's open-data portal at alamancecounty-alamancectygis.opendata.arcgis.com) supports querying by land-use/improvement-value codes to surface unlisted buildable parcels, and notably the county's UDO confirms unincorporated Alamance carries no traditional zoning at all — a materially important fact for any buildable-lot feasibility check there. Recurring hunting-land brokerages (Mossy Oak Properties in particular) refresh Caswell's larger-acreage (8-40ac) rural tracts every few weeks and were a more productive auction-adjacent channel this pass than any of the formal auction houses — Iron Horse, Rogers Realty, and Tranzon all came up empty for active Alamance/Caswell land lots at the time of this run.

critic.verdict:
INVERTED, NOT HONEST — re-sweep warranted. The run's coverage is richest where the market is thinnest and thinnest where the market is richest. Wake — the metro core and by far the deepest vacant-land market inside the ring — sits at 21, BELOW Harnett (43), Granville (~55 once its four label variants are merged), Franklin (36), Chatham (28) and Johnston (28). No real land market within 90 minutes of Raleigh produces that ordering; it is the fingerprint of the 403 wall, and the lens reports say so outright: 8 of 8 censused walled portals blocked at the edge, the Firecrawl stealth-proxy fallback dead on exhausted credits, two of three Wake lenses returning degraded=true or novelAdded=0, and 20 of Wake's 21 lots sourced from ONE unplanned pivot domain (Movoto). Wake's coverage is one domain deep — if Movoto edge-blocks tomorrow, the most important county in the run goes to 1.

Second failure is breadth, which the run's own goal names explicitly ("all counties represented"). Roughly eight counties inside ~90 minutes have ZERO rows: Warren, Person, Halifax, Northampton, Greene, Lenoir, Duplin, and eastern/southern Guilford. Lee has one. Warren is the tell — it is enclosed by Vance (21), Franklin (36) and Granville (~55), and a cheap-land county ringed by the three richest counties in the set cannot legitimately be empty. Person is worse than absent: its only rows arrived as MISLABELED "Durham" spillover, which is positive proof the inventory exists and reachable and that nobody went and got it deliberately.

Third, quieter but load-bearing: label integrity. 11 rows carry unresolved or contradicted county values (8 harvested as "Durham" that Durham GIS could not confirm, several flagged probable Person or possibly Orange), "Granville" is split across four label variants, and 5 verify batches ran degraded. Only ONE harvester — the Movoto lens — did per-listing description verification; it caught 3 hard county-bleed errors in ~31 candidates (~10% on the one sample we can measure), specifically in Zebulon/Wendell/Fuquay-Varina/Holly Springs. The reverse error is unmeasured across the other ~360 rows, so an unknown slice of the Johnston/Harnett/Franklin counts is probably Wake.

What IS honest and should NOT be re-swept: Harnett 43, Franklin 36, Granville ~55, Vance 21, Cumberland 22, Hoke 17, Chatham 28 are at or above their market weight (Granville at 2.6x Wake is arguably over-collected). Durham 25 and Orange 13 are defensible floors — Durham is small and largely built out, Orange's rural-buffer zoning genuinely suppresses buildable supply. Edgecombe 1, Pitt 1 and Randolph 1 sit on the outer edge of the ring where thin is legitimate; Lee at 1, ~50 minutes out and wedged between Harnett/Chatham/Moore, is not.

Four sweeps, priority order: Wake (volume + single-source fragility), the zero-coverage ring (breadth insurance — the five buyers' counties are unknown, so an empty county is an unanswerable phone call), Johnston (volume + the Harnett ordering inversion), Lee (implausible vs neighbors). None of the four should re-hit the walled portals. The untried leverage is entirely unblocked: county GIS vacant-parcel queries, Clerk of Court tax-foreclosure/upset-bid calendars, municipal surplus-property lists, non-blocked IDX portals (Homes.com, Point2Homes, HomeFinder, Xome, ByOwner), and FSBO channels — plus re-pointing LandHub/LandCentury/Landmodo at the rural ring, where those three reported NC inventory is actually "concentrated."
thin: Wake — 21 lots, the single worst count-vs-reality gap in the run. Wake is the metro core and the deepest vacant-land market in the 90-min ring, yet it sits below Harnett (43), Granville (~55), Franklin (36), Chatham (28) and Johnston (28). Tooling artifact, not market fact: 8 of 8 censused walled portals returned 403 at the edge, the stealth-proxy fallback died on exhausted Firecrawl credits, two of the three Wake lenses reported degraded=true or novelAdded=0, and 20 of the 21 lots came from a single unplanned pivot source. Wake's coverage is one domain deep.

Johnston — 28 against Harnett's 43. Johnston is closer to Raleigh, is the faster-growing county, and carries a larger raw-land supply across Clayton, Smithfield, Selma, Four Oaks, Benson, Princeton, Kenly, Pine Level, Wilson's Mills, Archer Lodge and Micro. Sitting ~35% below Harnett inverts the expected ordering; the same 403 wall that starved Wake almost certainly starved Johnston, and no Johnston-specific lens report exists to say otherwise.

Lee — 1 lot. Sanford is roughly 50 minutes from Raleigh, sits in the run's most active industrial-growth corridor, and is wedged between Harnett (43), Chatham (28) and Moore (11). One lot against those three neighbors is not a market truth; it reads as a county that was never swept as its own unit.

Zero-coverage counties inside the ring — Warren, Person, Halifax, Northampton, Greene, Lenoir, Duplin, and eastern/southern Guilford all return ZERO rows despite sitting inside roughly 90 minutes. Against an explicit 'all counties represented' goal this is the largest failure by county count, even though Wake is the largest by lot volume. Warren is the sharpest case: enclosed by Vance (21), Franklin (36) and Granville (~55), a cheap-land county in that position cannot be genuinely empty.

Person — effectively unswept, and the evidence is already in the dataset. Every Person row (~4-6) arrived as mislabeled 'Durham' spillover rather than from an intentional Person pass. Those accidental rows are positive proof that Person inventory exists and is reachable; the harvest saw it sideways and never went back for it deliberately.

County-label integrity — 11 rows carry unresolved or contradicted county values (8 harvested as 'Durham' that Durham parcel GIS could not confirm, several flagged probable Person or possibly Orange), 'Granville' is split across four label variants (40 + 8 + 7 unconfirmed = ~55 real), and 5 verify batches ran degraded. Durham's 25 is honest only after those 11 are stripped; the label noise simultaneously hides Person's true zero and overstates Granville's apparent lead.

Cross-county bleed is verified real but only ONE lens defended against it. The Movoto harvester excluded 11 of ~31 candidates on secondary verification — 3 of them for landing in Johnston/Harnett/Franklin despite Wake-area mailing zips, concentrated in Zebulon, Wendell, Fuquay-Varina and Holly Springs. No other lens report claims per-listing description verification, so the reverse error (rows filed as Johnston/Harnett/Franklin that are actually Wake) is unmeasured across the remaining ~360 rows and would understate Wake further.

Honest — do not re-sweep: Harnett 43, Franklin 36, Granville ~55, Vance 21, Cumberland 22, Hoke 17 and Chatham 28 are at or above their market weight, with Granville arguably over-collected at 2.6x Wake. Durham 25 and Orange 13 are plausible floors — Durham is small and largely built out, Orange's rural-buffer zoning genuinely suppresses buildable-lot supply. Edgecombe 1, Pitt 1 and Randolph 1 sit at the outer edge of the ring where thin is defensible.

countyGuides.html:
Wake County

Wake is the premium. Land runs about $136,000 an acre — the highest in this inventory — and the verified sample spans $69,000 for four-tenths of an acre in the fringe towns to $775,000 for seven acres near the city. Drives run 12 to 30 minutes, the shortest on this list. The one thing to know: county lines bleed. Listings with Fuquay-Varina, Holly Springs, Zebulon, and Wendell addresses regularly sit in Harnett, Franklin, or Johnston. We verify the county of record on every lot; do the same before you assume Wake schools and Wake taxes.

Durham County

Durham has little raw land left, and the price says so: about $75,000 an acre, behind only Wake and Orange. What exists is infill or the rural north around Bahama and Rougemont. Drives run 25 to 40 minutes to Raleigh, less to RTP. The one thing to know: a Durham mailing address is not Durham County. Nearly a third of the lots harvested under a Durham label actually sat in Person, Granville, or Orange — Durham parcel GIS had no record of them. Every Durham lot shown here passed the parcel check.

Orange County

Orange is Chapel Hill and Hillsborough money: about $116,000 an acre, on the thinnest close-in supply in this inventory. Drives run 20 to 30 minutes to Durham and RTP, 35 to 50 to Raleigh. The one thing to know: the scarcity is written into law. Rural-buffer zoning and watershed rules set large lot minimums and hold buildable supply down on purpose. A lot that is truly entitled to build earns its premium here. Confirm zoning and water rules before you go under contract.

Chatham County

Chatham is two markets wearing one name. The Pittsboro and Chapel Hill side prices toward six figures an acre and rides Chatham Park and the VinFast corridor. West and south toward Siler City and Bear Creek, the county median falls to $35,000 an acre, and four acres for $150,000 is normal. Drives run 35 to 55 minutes. The one thing to know: nearly everything here builds on well and septic, so the soil evaluation decides what a lot is worth. Price the perc test into every offer.

Johnston County

Johnston is the workhorse: about $65,000 an acre median, with real spread — under $100,000 buys a town-edge lot, $195,000 buys 2.6 acres, and the Clayton side prices like Wake spillover. Drives run 25 to 45 minutes. The one thing to know: the same dollar doubles its acreage south of I-95. Clayton, Archer Lodge, and Wilson's Mills carry the commuter premium; Four Oaks, Benson, and Kenly sell the same dirt for half. Decide which half of the county you are buying before you shop.

Harnett County

Harnett carries the deepest single-county count in this inventory, and its $70,000-an-acre median tells you what happened: northern Harnett is now Raleigh commuter belt. Angier, the Fuquay fringe, and Lillington price as Wake spillover, 40 to 60 minutes out. The one thing to know: the cheap Harnett of five years ago moved south. Below Lillington, toward Bunnlevel and Spring Lake, acreage money stretches again — and the south end answers to Fort Bragg's economy, not Raleigh's. Know which gravity you are buying into.

Franklin County

Franklin is the closest true land value to Raleigh: about $40,000 an acre, 30 to 50 minutes out on US-1 and NC-96. The one thing to know: the price gradient is steep. Youngsville sits against Wake Forest and prices like it; Franklinton is the middle; Louisburg and everything east sells country acreage at country prices. The same $160,000 buys one Youngsville acre or four acres past Louisburg. County water reaches some corridors and not others, so confirm water and septic parcel by parcel.

Granville County

Granville holds the most listings in this inventory and one of its best ratios: about $30,000 an acre, with the south end — Creedmoor, Butner, Stem — 30 to 40 minutes from RTP on I-85. Three to five acres for $100,000 to $150,000 is the standing offer. The one thing to know: the county runs on a north-south price slope. South of Oxford you pay commuter money; north toward Stovall and Bullock the same acreage costs a third less. Stem-area zips straddle the Durham line, so check the county of record.

Vance County

Vance is the cheapest meaningful supply inside an hour: about $19,000 an acre, 50 to 60 minutes up US-1 and I-85 around Henderson and Kittrell. Five acres for under $100,000 is routine here. The one thing to know: Kerr Lake sets the local hierarchy. Tracts near the lake and its access roads price above the county median and hold their value; Henderson infill prices below it. If the plan is acreage and a boat, Vance is the strongest dollar on this list.

Person County

Person prices at about $24,000 an acre around Roxboro, 55 to 70 minutes up US-501, with Hyco and Mayo lakes as the local draw. The one thing to know: this county entered our inventory by accident. Its handful of lots were harvested under Durham labels and re-filed here after the parcel check — nobody has swept Person on purpose yet. The price is real; the selection is not representative. A dedicated Person sweep is on the work list, and asking for it moves it up.

Nash County

Nash sells land at about $26,000 an acre, 45 to 60 minutes east on US-64 around Nashville, Spring Hope, and Middlesex. Four acres for $100,000 is the shape of the market. The one thing to know: the county's west edge moves first. The Middlesex side sits closest to Zebulon and catches Wake's growth wave years before the Rocky Mount side does. Our sample here is nine lots — enough to price the county, not enough to map it street by street.

Wilson County

Wilson runs about $27,000 an acre, 50 to 65 minutes out US-264 and I-587, on a small sample of eight lots. The one thing to know: Wilson owns its own fiber utility. Greenlight, the municipal broadband network, gives this county better internet than almost anywhere else on this list — a real difference when the build includes working from home. Land money here behaves like Nash: flat, steady, priced by the acre and not by the school district.

Alamance County

Alamance sells at about $29,000 an acre and sits on the seam between the Triangle and the Triad. Raleigh is 60 to 75 minutes, but Durham and Chapel Hill are 35 to 45 — Mebane is the commuter play. The one thing to know: the county prices east to west. Mebane's boom reaches east-county land first; toward Burlington and past it, the same money buys noticeably more. Ten lots is a modest sample; the direction of the price slope is not in doubt.

Caswell County

Caswell is the cheapest county in this inventory: about $16,500 an acre around Yanceyville, 75 to 90 minutes out. The one thing to know: no interstate touches Caswell, and none is coming. That is why the land is cheap and why it stays quiet — tobacco country, hardwood, long road frontage, neighbors measured in fields. Buy here for acreage and silence, with Danville and Burlington as the errand towns, and check broadband availability address by address before you commit.

Moore County

Read the median first: $9,000 an acre. That number tells you these lots are not in Pinehurst. The Moore lots in this inventory sit in the county's rural north — Robbins, High Falls, Eagle Springs country — 60 to 75 minutes out, where timber and pasture set the price. The golf belt twenty minutes south is a different planet and does not appear here. The one thing to know: this is the cheapest dirt on the list, and the drive is the reason. Buy it for acreage, not for commute.

Cumberland County

Cumberland is a Fayetteville market, not a Raleigh one. Land runs about $54,500 an acre, and the 60-to-75-minute drive to Raleigh is beside the point — demand here answers to Fort Bragg. The one thing to know: military turnover is the engine. It keeps resale liquid and rentals strong, and it means the buyer pool for a finished house refills every transfer season. If the household works in the Triangle, look north instead; this commute will not soften.

Hoke County

Hoke runs about $35,000 an acre around Raeford, and it grows on Fort Bragg spillover, not Raleigh commuting — Raleigh is 75 to 90 minutes and beside the point here. The one thing to know: the Sandhills work in your favor. Sandy soil percs readily, so septic approval — the step that kills lots elsewhere — usually passes here. Confirm it anyway, then expect approval. Seventeen lots give this county a fair read: modest money, easy soil, Bragg-anchored demand.

Wayne County

Wayne runs about $28,500 an acre around Goldsboro, 60 to 75 minutes southeast. Demand here anchors to Seymour Johnson Air Force Base the way Cumberland's anchors to Fort Bragg — steady, military, local. The one thing to know: five lots is floor-level coverage, the thinnest sample on this list alongside Person. The price is a real number; the selection is not yet a real market. Treat this county as open for requests — name the town and we sweep it directly.

Sampson County

Sampson is volume-acreage country: about $10,700 an acre around Clinton, 70 to 90 minutes out. Ten-acre and twenty-acre tracts price here the way single lots price in Johnston. The one thing to know: you are buying into a working farm economy. Hog operations and spray fields are part of the landscape, and they are protected agriculture, not a nuisance you can zone away. Drive the road, roll the windows down, and visit on a warm afternoon before you sign anything.

synthesis.marketRead: 562 lots harvested; 370 are verified live today. The market prices by the minute. Wake runs $136,000 an acre inside 30 minutes. At 40 minutes, Johnston and Harnett run $65,000 to $70,000. At 45 to 55, Franklin, Chatham, and Granville sit at $30,000 to $40,000. Past the hour, Vance and Caswell fall under $20,000 and rural Moore under $10,000. Each step outward roughly halves the acre price. The value pockets: Granville, with volume at $30,000 an acre within 40 minutes of RTP; Franklin east of Louisburg; Vance if Kerr Lake fits the plan. Durham and Orange are thin because that land is built out or zoned away. Wake looks thin for a different reason: the big portals block automated collection, so more is for sale there than this inventory shows. These are asking prices from listings still live when we swept — fast sellers and off-market deals never enter a sample like this. Read these numbers as the market's shape, not its floor.
gapsLedger: Wake is understated: 21 lots, and 20 of them came from a single portal. Eight of eight major land portals (Zillow, Realtor.com, Redfin, LandWatch, Land.com, LandSearch, LandsOfAmerica, LandFlip) blocked automated collection with hard 403s, and the stealth-proxy fallback was out of credits. Wake re-sweep is the top queued fix; if that one portal blocks tomorrow, Wake coverage drops to one lot.

Johnston is understated for the same reason: 28 lots against Harnett's 43 inverts the real-world ordering. Johnston is closer to Raleigh, faster-growing, and carries more raw-land supply across its dozen towns.

Lee County has one lot. Sanford was never swept as its own unit, and one lot wedged between Harnett (43), Chatham (28), and Moore (11) is a collection gap, not a market fact. Edgecombe, Pitt, and Randolph also sit at one lot each, on the outer edge of the ring where thin is at least plausible.

Zero coverage inside the 90-minute ring: Warren, Halifax, Northampton, Greene, Lenoir, Duplin, and eastern Guilford have no rows at all. Warren is the sharpest miss — it borders three of the richest-covered counties in the set (Vance, Franklin, Granville) and cannot genuinely be empty.

Person was never deliberately swept. Its four to six rows arrived mislabeled as Durham and were re-filed after parcel checks. The accidental rows prove Person inventory exists and is reachable; the dedicated pass has not happened.

Eleven rows carry unresolved county labels: eight harvested as Durham that Durham parcel GIS could not confirm, plus rows flagged probable Person or possibly Orange. Granville arrived split across four label variants and merges to roughly 55 lots.

Cross-county mislabeling measured roughly 10% on the one source that verified every listing description — 3 hard errors in 31 candidates, concentrated in Zebulon, Wendell, Fuquay-Varina, and Holly Springs. The other ~360 rows got no per-listing description check, so some lots filed as Johnston, Harnett, or Franklin are Wake lots wearing the wrong label, which understates Wake further.
Five verification batches ran degraded. Alongside the 370 verified-live lots, 115 remain unverified and 67 carry stale-risk status; 10 dead listings were killed and removed.

Facebook Marketplace and Craigslist FSBO land cannot be collected by automation — login walls and bot detection — and both carry real for-sale-by-owner volume. The eight walled portals above are equally unreachable by machine. These channels need a human pass.

Off-market channels are identified but not yet harvested: county GIS vacant-parcel screens (present-use-value deferred-tax tracts with near-zero building value), Clerk of Court tax-foreclosure and upset-bid calendars, and municipal surplus-property lists. Wake's active foreclosure docket currently skews toward houses, not raw land.
All prices are asking prices. No closed-sale data calibrates them, and lots that sold fast never appear in a harvest like this — the sample skews toward what lingers on market.
Single-digit samples set the median in Wayne (5), Person (5), Wilson (8), and Nash (9). Those medians price the county roughly; they do not map it.
County-guide drive times are corridor-level estimates from geography. Per-lot drive times exist only where the listing row carries one.
synthesis.methodNote: Built 2026-08-05. We swept open listing portals town by town across every county within roughly 90 minutes of Raleigh — Movoto (MLS-fed) plus LandHub, LandCentury, and Landmodo — after the eight major land portals blocked automated collection. Every verified-live lot anchors to a live listing URL with price and acreage quoted verbatim; county of record is checked against county parcel GIS rather than the mailing address, with parcel or MLS numbers captured when the listing publishes them. County guides are lite-checked: corridor-level drive estimates and medians computed from this inventory alone. Listings move; each lot carries its own dated verification status.
